section.name: JNDI Howto
section.p: The Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) is part of the Java platform, providing applications based on Java technology with a unified interface to multiple naming and directory services. You can build powerful and portable directory-enabled applications using this industry standard.

When you deploy your application inside an application server, the container will setup the JNDI tree for you. But if you are writing a framework or just a standalone application, then the following examples will show you how to construct and bind references to DBCP datasources.
The following examples are using the sun filesystem JNDI service provider. You can download it from the JNDI software download page.

section.name: BasicDataSource
DriverAdapterCPDS password export
section.p: Since 2.15.0, DriverAdapterCPDS.setExportPasswordAsRefAddr(false) omits the dedicated password address from References produced by getReference(), including when a naming provider binds the data source through Referenceable. Export remains enabled by default for compatibility. Protect References containing credentials and any directory entries, logs, backups, or replication streams that store them.

When export is disabled, a newly reconstructed data source has no default password. Supply it with setPassword() before the first connection attempt, even an unsuccessful one, or pass credentials to getPooledConnection(user, password). A container that looks up and immediately uses the data source must supply credentials through its own configuration or retain export. For example, an application that performs the lookup itself can provision the resolved instance before handing it to its pool:

The export setting is retained through lookup and rebinding, so provisioning the resolved password does not re-enable export. A manually constructed Reference can configure it with a StringRefAddr("exportPasswordAsRefAddr", "false"); this controls future exports and does not prevent the factory from reading a supplied password address. Other addresses, including credentials embedded in JDBC URLs, remain unchanged. Java serialization still contains the configured password. Changing the setting does not remove credentials from previously created References or directory entries.
